text: Welcome to module three.

In the last module, you explored how to define requirements
and build test cases,

and you saw how to review the results manually for errors
and group similar mistakes together.

Reviewing results manually helps you develop a nuanced understanding
of where an application falls short of its requirements.
When you personally see how it goes wrong and what details matter,

you can use that understanding to make more informed decisions about
what needs to improve.

But manual review takes time and focused attention, and the more test
cases you run, the more responses you have to review.
That makes it hard to keep doing every review by hand.

As you saw in module one, you can evaluate results yourself
through human review,

but you can also automate those checks using code
evaluators and LLM judges.

So in this module, you'll learn about those automated evaluators
so you can check more responses without reviewing each one yourself.

You'll also learn how to test whether the evaluators are making the
right judgments. Let's start in this video with code evaluators.

Once you run a test case, you have a response to check
against a requirement.

A code evaluator makes that check programmatically with ordinary code,
using rules that specify exactly what counts as a pass or a failure.

So, when should you use a code evaluator? The key is whether you can
program an explicit rule that determines the answer.

For example, if a response must stay under 500 characters,
you can count the characters and compare the total with the limit.
There's no judgment call about whether it's short enough.

Contrast that with evaluating whether a response from the shelter app
clearly explains why a dog is a bad match for a volunteer.

You need to consider what the response says and whether the
explanation is clear.

So this kind of evaluation requires interpretation and is better
suited to a human or an LLM judge.

So code evaluators fit questions where a specific rule or calculation
is enough to determine whether the requirement was met.

So that might include checking whether a required step ran,
whether a claim matches the records,
or whether a response includes all the required fields.
So how do you turn one of those checks into a code evaluator?

You can simply write a Python function that applies deterministic
logic to information from the trace.

Every code evaluator follows the same pattern: it takes inputs,
runs your evaluation logic, and returns an output.

For a response check, the inputs might be the request and response
from a span passed to the function as text.
Other checks may need a database record or details of a tool call.

The output is the evaluator's judgment, such as a score of 1 with a
pass label or 0 with a fail label.

The particular check you want to make is the logic you
write in the middle.

For example, in the shelter app, the agent should reject a volunteer
who is flagged in the do not adopt records.

Your function needs the volunteer ID, the corresponding record,
and the agent's decision.

If the record flags the volunteer, but the agent approved them,
evaluator returns a fail label and a score of 0.

Because the rule determines the result, the evaluator does not need an
LLM to make the judgment.

A code evaluator may be a simple Python function,
but that doesn't mean the work inside it has to be simple.

You're not limited to string operations,
such as matching words in a response.

You can call an API, query a database, or perform any deterministic
check you can write in code.

For the shelter's volunteer check, the function first retrieves the
trace through an API call.

The trace gives it the volunteer ID and the agent's decision.
The function then uses that ID to query the do not adopt records.

Once the function has the record and the agent's decision,
it returns a fail if a flagged volunteer wasn't rejected.

So this evaluator involves an API call, a database query,
and several lines of logic.

What makes it a code evaluator isn't how simple the check is,
but that the check is deterministic.

The logic can be as detailed as the requirement demands, and given the
same trace and the same record, it will return the same judgment.

Code evaluators aren't limited to checking decisions.
You can also check whether the agent took the required steps.

For example, the shelter agent might correctly approve a volunteer,
but the trace shows it never checked the do-not-adopt records.

You can write an evaluator that looks for that required lookup in the
trace, and returns a fail if it's missing,
even though the final decision was correct.
Let's look at a few more examples from the shelter app.

You can use code for format checks, such as whether the shelter agent
returns valid JSON and includes the volunteer ID, dog ID,
and approval status.

You can check whether the response stays within a length limit
or contains a prohibited phrase, such as "as an AI assistant."

And you can check facts against the records and required steps against
the trace. Does the volunteer ID exist in the system?

Does the dog's reported eligibility match its record? Did the agent
check the do-not-adopt records before approving the volunteer?
These checks don't have to be brittle.

When you're comparing text, you can normalize whitespace,
ignore capitalization where it doesn't matter,

or write the check to accept valid alternative wording,
so a response doesn't fail just because it uses a different phrase.

So when an explicit rule or calculation can determine whether a
requirement was met, you can automate that check with code.

That makes code a useful first line of defense. You can catch a clear
violation without making or paying for an LLM call.

Even a simple record check can catch a serious mistake,
such as approving a flagged volunteer.

Code evaluators and LLM judges also fit into the same
evaluation workflow.

You retrieve the recorded runs, pass each evaluator the information it
needs, and save its scores and labels with the run it evaluated.

In Phoenix, you can log both kinds of judgment as annotations on the
same trace so you can see the evaluations together.

But some requirements call for interpreting what a
response means in context.

You might need to judge whether an explanation is clear,
whether a response is empathetic,
or whether a recommendation addresses someone's needs.
Those judgments depend on how the response fits the situation,

so counting characters or checking that a field is
present won't be enough.

You've already explored how to make judgments like these
through human review.

In the next video, you'll learn how to use an LLM judge to evaluate
responses against requirements that call for interpretation.
